findings.title: Unguarded Admin Data-Fetch Actions Expose All Buyer PII
findings.description: getAdminStats(), getAdminProducts(), getAdminPools(), getAdminPool(), and getAdminOrders() perform NO authentication or authorization check. They are Server Actions exposed as POST endpoints. getAdminOrders() (line 238) returns every buyer's full_name, phone, address, company_name joined across all orders. Any authenticated buyer (not just admins) can call these directly.
findings.impact: Any logged-in buyer can enumerate ALL buyer PII (phone numbers, addresses, company names) and full order history for every customer. getAdminOrders() is especially critical — it joins profiles to pool_orders and returns full PII for every user in the database.
findings.exploit:
1. Log in as a regular buyer account.
2. Open browser DevTools > Network tab.
3. Find the Server Action chunk ID for 'getAdminOrders' in the JS bundle (or trigger it from an admin page if temporarily accessible).
4. POST to the Next.js server action endpoint with the correct action ID and credentials cookie.
5. Receive JSON response containing all user phone numbers, addresses, and order data.

Alternatively, since these functions have no auth guard, RLS IS the only protection. However, the server-side Supabase client uses the anon key — so RLS policies DO apply. But getAdminOrders() runs with the session of the calling user. If the calling user is authenticated but not admin, the query would fail at RLS on profiles (admin-only SELECT policy). This partially mitigates the risk, but the LACK of explicit server-side auth guard is still a design flaw that relies entirely on RLS being correct — with no defense-in-depth.
findings.rls_mitigation: RLS on pool_orders allows SELECT only for own orders OR admin. RLS on profiles allows SELECT only for own profile OR admin. So a non-admin buyer calling getAdminOrders() via a crafted request would receive empty results (not error) due to RLS, NOT a full dump. However, the function still executes and the lack of authorization guard is a serious defense-in-depth failure.
findings.fix: Add 'await requireAdmin()' as the first line inside getAdminStats(), getAdminProducts(), getAdminPools(), getAdminPool(), and getAdminOrders().
findings.status: CONFIRMED — Design flaw (missing explicit guard). Practical data exposure partially mitigated by RLS, but is still a P1 finding due to defense-in-depth failure.

findings.title: Rate Limiter IP Spoofing via X-Forwarded-For Header
findings.description: The rate limiter extracts the client IP directly from the 'x-forwarded-for' HTTP header without any validation or trusted-proxy configuration. An attacker can set this header to any arbitrary value to bypass rate limiting on login, signup, and password reset endpoints.
findings.impact: An attacker can attempt unlimited login attempts against any account by rotating the X-Forwarded-For header. This enables brute force attacks against user passwords, including the admin account.
findings.exploit:
1. Identify a target email (e.g., admin@bharatbrand.com).
2. Write a script that POSTs to the login Server Action with different X-Forwarded-For values on each request:
   curl -X POST [url] -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.X' -d 'email=admin@...&password=guess'
3. Rotate X between 1-255 to get effectively unlimited attempts.
4. The in-memory Map stores keys as IP:action, so each new spoofed IP gets a fresh 5-attempt window.
5. Additionally, on Vercel/serverless, the in-memory Map resets on every cold start, making the rate limiter completely ineffective between Lambda invocations.
findings.fix:
1. On Vercel/production: use Upstash Redis with @upstash/ratelimit for distributed rate limiting.
2. Use the LAST entry in x-forwarded-for (the rightmost untrusted hop) or use a trusted proxy configuration.
3. Consider using Supabase Auth's built-in rate limiting for auth endpoints instead of a custom implementation.
4. Add account lockout at the Supabase level.

findings.title: In-Memory Rate Limiter is Ineffective on Serverless/Vercel
findings.description: The rate limiter uses a module-level in-memory Map. On Vercel serverless, each Lambda invocation may use a different instance, and instances are recycled frequently. The rate limit state is NOT shared across instances. A comment in the file itself acknowledges this: 'Simple in-memory rate limiting for development. In production, replace with @upstash/ratelimit and Redis'.
findings.impact: Login brute force protection is non-existent in production. The file's own comment warns this should not be used in production. An attacker attempting 5+ logins may simply hit a different Lambda instance with a fresh count.
findings.exploit:
1. Send 5 login attempts from the same IP — rate limit triggers.
2. Wait ~30 seconds for Lambda to recycle.
3. Send 5 more attempts — counter is at 0 again.
4. Repeat indefinitely.
findings.fix: Implement distributed rate limiting using Upstash Redis: 'npm install @upstash/ratelimit @upstash/redis'. Use sliding window rate limiting tied to both IP and email for auth endpoints.

findings.title: joinPool() Does Not Validate Input Against JoinPoolSchema
findings.description: The JoinPoolSchema exists in validations.ts (line 3-6) and validates poolId as UUID and quantity as positive integer. However, joinPool() (line 60) never calls JoinPoolSchema.safeParse(). The function accepts any poolId string and any quantity integer without format validation.
findings.impact:
1. An attacker can pass quantity=0 or negative numbers if the parseInt() parsing allows it. Currently the client sends parsed integers, but a direct server action call can bypass client-side min attributes.
2. An attacker can pass non-UUID poolId strings — the DB query will gracefully return null, but the lack of early validation is a defense gap.
3. If quantity can be 0 or negative: the pool's current_quantity gets decremented (pool.current_quantity + quantity where quantity is negative), potentially corrupting pool state.
findings.exploit: Craft a direct POST to the joinPool server action with quantity=-100. If not blocked by DB constraints, this decrements pool.current_quantity.
findings.rls_note: The pool_orders table has CHECK constraints on quantity (NOT NULL) and the INSERT with negative quantity may violate DB integrity. However, no explicit DB CHECK constraint on quantity > 0 is defined in the schema.
findings.fix: Add at the top of joinPool(): 'const validated = JoinPoolSchema.safeParse({ poolId, quantity }); if (!validated.success) return { error: "Invalid input" };'
findings.status: CONFIRMED — quantity=-999 would be passed to DB insert. Whether DB rejects it depends on constraints not visible in the schema (no explicit CHECK quantity > 0 defined).

findings.title: Verbose Debug Logging of Sensitive Data in Production Server Actions
findings.description: Extensive console.log() debug statements are left in production server action code. These log: user IDs, pool IDs, quantities, tier pricing data, insert payloads, DB error messages with codes/hints/details, profile data (full_name, phone, company_name, address), and exception stack traces.
findings.impact:
1. Vercel/server logs (accessible to anyone with project access) contain user PII and sensitive business data.
2. order.ts line 138 logs the full exception stack trace: 'console.log(10a. Stack: e.stack)' — stack traces reveal internal file paths, library versions.
3. profile.ts line 40 logs: { full_name, phone, company_name, address } — raw PII in logs.
4. order.ts line 122 returns raw DB error to client: 'DB: ${insertError.message} (code: ${insertError.code})' — exposes internal DB error messages to the browser.
findings.exploit:
1. Gain read access to Vercel logs (compromised developer account, insider threat, log aggregation leak).
2. Read full PII for all users who updated profiles or joined pools.
3. For item 4: trigger an error in joinPool() and receive DB schema information in the browser response.
findings.fix:
1. Remove all console.log() debug statements from order.ts and profile.ts.
2. Replace with logger.info/warn/error() using sanitized data (no PII, no raw stack traces).
3. In joinPool() line 121-123: return generic error message instead of raw DB error string.
4. In profile.ts line 75: return 'Database error' not 'Database error: ' + error.message.

findings.title: Middleware Auth Function Named 'proxy' — Semantic Confusion Risk
findings.description: The main middleware function is exported as 'proxy' (line 4: 'export async function proxy(request)') and also as 'export default proxy'. The comment on line 19 states 'Next.js 16 requires a default or named middleware export'. The actual middleware logic in lib/supabase/middleware.ts is called 'updateSession'. The proxy function adds security headers and calls updateSession. This naming is not a direct vulnerability but creates confusion about what the middleware does.
findings.impact: Low — naming confusion could lead future developers to bypass the proxy function when adding middleware logic, thinking it's only a proxy/header-setter.
findings.fix: Rename the function from 'proxy' to 'middleware' for clarity: 'export async function middleware(request)' and 'export default middleware'.

findings.title: CSP Contains 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval' — XSS Amplification
findings.description: The Content-Security-Policy header includes 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval' for script-src. This means any XSS injection (even reflected) can execute arbitrary JavaScript without CSP blocking it.
findings.impact: If an XSS vector is found (e.g., in product name/description rendered without escaping), the CSP provides zero protection.
findings.fix: Use a nonce-based CSP instead of 'unsafe-inline'. Next.js supports nonce-based CSP via middleware. Remove 'unsafe-eval' — it is not needed for React/Next.js in production.

findings.title: Admin Data-Read Functions Callable by Any Authenticated User (Defense-in-Depth Gap)
findings.description: See FINDING-001 for full details. Classified separately to distinguish the 'design gap' aspect (no explicit auth guard in the function) from the practical exploitability (partially blocked by RLS). Even though RLS filters results, calling getAdminOrders() as a buyer returns an empty array rather than an error, leaking the existence of the endpoint and its structure.
findings.impact: Information disclosure: endpoint structure, column names in error scenarios, existence confirmation of data.
findings.fix: Add requireAdmin() to all admin data-fetch functions (not just mutating ones).

findings.title: anon Key in .env.local is Public by Design — but Committed URL is Live
findings.description: The NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY in .env.local are intentionally public (NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix embeds them in the JS bundle). The anon key has been confirmed to be a JWT with role:anon — not service_role. The .gitignore correctly includes '.env*' so this file should not be committed to a remote repository. However, the project is synced via OneDrive which is not git-controlled.
findings.impact: The anon key is safe to be public. No secret exposure. RLS protects the database.
findings.fix: No code change needed. Verify that .env.local is NOT committed to any remote git repository by running: git log --all -- .env.local
findings.status: REJECTED — anon key is designed to be public. No service_role key present. .gitignore correctly excludes .env files.

findings.title: Next.js CVE-2025-29927 Middleware Bypass Check
findings.description: CVE-2025-29927 affected Next.js versions < 15.2.3, allowing middleware bypass via the x-middleware-subrequest header. The application uses Next.js 16.3.3.
findings.impact: Not affected. Next.js 16.3.3 is well above the patched version 15.2.3.
findings.status: REJECTED — Not vulnerable. Version 16.3.3 > 15.2.3 patched version.

findings.title: Slopsquatting / Package Verification
findings.description: All dependencies verified: next@16.3.3, react@19.2.8, @supabase/ssr@^0.12.5, @supabase/supabase-js@^2.112.4, zod@^4.5.1, tailwindcss@^4.0.0, puppeteer@^25.9.0. All are legitimate, widely-used packages published by known organizations on npm. No hallucinated or suspicious package names detected.

findings.title: IDOR on getOrderById / getOrderDetails — PROTECTED
findings.description: Both getOrderById() and getOrderDetails() correctly filter by both order ID AND buyer_id = user.id. An attacker navigating to /checkout/[someone-elses-order-id] will receive null and see the notFound() page.

findings.title: Profile Update IDOR — PROTECTED
findings.description: updateProfile() upserts with 'id: user.id' where user.id comes from supabase.auth.getUser() — a server-side, session-validated call. The user cannot set their own ID to another user's ID. RLS additionally enforces UPDATE USING (auth.uid() = id).
findings.status: REJECTED — Profile update IDOR is properly protected

findings.title: Cookie Security — HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite
findings.description: Supabase SSR (@supabase/ssr) manages auth cookies. Supabase sets HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite=Lax by default on auth tokens. Next.js Server Actions are inherently protected against cross-origin CSRF because they require same-origin cookies and the Content-Type: text/plain header for cross-origin requests. Server Actions verify the Origin header automatically in Next.js 13+.
findings.status: REJECTED — Cookie security and CSRF protection handled by framework defaults
